lead: A graph is a set of vertices and a set of edges, where each edge joins two vertices. This simple object captures pairwise relations: roads between towns, flights between airports, links between web pages, or matches between cricket teams. The same idea answers practical questions: how many handshakes happen, whether a network splits into two groups, or how many links a complete network needs. This chapter fixes the vocabulary and the standard graph families that later chapters use for paths, colouring, trees and shortest routes.
prereq: You need Unit 2, Sets, Relations and Functions for vertex and edge sets, and Unit 3 for simple counting.

blocks.text: A graph G = (V, E) has a vertex set V and an edge set E. In a simple undirected graph each edge is a two-element subset {u, v}, written uv; in a multigraph or pseudograph an edge is an unordered pair of endpoints that may repeat or have u = v. The endpoints u and v are adjacent. A simple graph has no loops and no parallel edges. A multigraph allows two or more parallel edges between the same pair. A pseudograph also allows a loop, an edge from a vertex to itself. A directed graph, or digraph, has ordered edges (u, v): the edge points from u to v. The indegree indeg(v) counts edges entering v; the outdegree outdeg(v) counts edges leaving v. A graph need not be connected; connectivity is studied in 6.3.
The degree deg(v) is the number of edge ends at v. A loop adds 2, because both ends meet the same vertex. The handshaking lemma connects degrees to the edge count.

blocks.where: V is the vertex set; E is the edge set; deg(v) is the degree of vertex v; |E| is the number of edges.

blocks.text: Proof: each edge has two ends, so it contributes 2 to the total of all degrees. Therefore the degree sum is always even. The degree sequence is the list of degrees in non-increasing order; for a simple graph on n vertices every entry is between 0 and n−1. In a digraph, Σ indeg(v) = Σ outdeg(v) = |E|, because every directed edge has one tail and one head.

blocks.text: In K<sub>n</sub> every pair of distinct vertices is joined, so each vertex has degree n−1. C<sub>n</sub> is a single cycle of n vertices. W<sub>n</sub> here means one hub joined to every vertex of C<sub>n−1</sub>; some syllabi use n+1 vertices, so check the convention. Q<sub>n</sub> has bit strings of length n as vertices, with edges between strings that differ in exactly one bit.

A graph is bipartite when V can be split into X and Y so every edge has one end in X and the other in Y. K<sub>m,n</sub> is the complete bipartite graph: all mn edges between the two parts exist. A bipartite graph has no odd cycle; a triangle is the usual obstruction. A graph is r-regular when every vertex has degree r. K<sub>n</sub> is (n−1)-regular, C<sub>n</sub> is 2-regular, and Q<sub>n</sub> is n-regular.

Some syllabi list graph operations. A subgraph uses a subset of vertices and a subset of edges among them. The union of two graphs on the same vertex set combines their edge sets. The complement has the same vertices and exactly the edges missing from the original simple graph. Matrix storage and isomorphism are in 6.2.

examples.question: For the graph G with vertex set V = {A, B, C, D} and edge set E = {AB, AC, BC, CD}: (a) list deg(v) for each vertex; (b) verify the handshaking lemma; (c) decide whether G is bipartite.
steps: Read each edge as two incidences. AB gives one to A and one to B; AC gives one to A and one to C; BC gives one to B and one to C; CD gives one to C and one to D.
Count: deg(A) = 2 (AB, AC), deg(B) = 2 (AB, BC), deg(C) = 3 (AC, BC, CD), deg(D) = 1 (CD).
Sum = 2 + 2 + 3 + 1 = 8. Here |E| = 4, so 2|E| = 8. The lemma holds.
Bipartite test: the triangle A-B-C is a cycle of length 3. A bipartite graph has no odd cycle. So G is not bipartite.
examples.answer: The degrees are A=2, B=2, C=3 and D=1; their sum is 8 = 2 × 4, so the handshaking lemma holds, and the graph is not bipartite because A-B-C is a triangle.

traps: The handshaking lemma says Σ deg(v) = 2|E|, not |E|. A sum equal to |E| means you forgot the factor 2.
A loop adds 2 to the degree of its vertex, not 1, because both ends of the loop meet the same vertex.
K<sub>m,n</sub> has mn edges, not m+n. The value m+n is the number of vertices.
Bipartite forbids every odd cycle, not every cycle. C<sub>4</sub> is bipartite; C<sub>3</sub> is not.
W<sub>n</sub> notation varies: some books use n vertices (hub plus C<sub>n−1</sub>), others use n+1 vertices (hub plus C<sub>n</sub>). Check the definition in the question.

quiz.q: State the handshaking lemma. Define deg(v) in a pseudograph.
quiz.a: Σ deg(v) = 2|E|. deg(v) is the number of edge ends at v; a loop counts twice.
C<sub>5</sub> is an odd cycle. In a bipartite graph colours alternate along a cycle, so every cycle has even length.

quiz.q: For K<sub>4</sub>, find the number of edges and the degree of each vertex.
quiz.a: Edges = 4·3/2 = 6. Each vertex is joined to the other 3, so every degree is 3.

quiz.q: A simple graph has 7 edges. Six of its vertices have degrees 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3. Find the seventh degree.
quiz.a: Degree sum = 2 × 7 = 14. The six known degrees sum to 1+1+2+2+3+3 = 12. The seventh degree is 14 − 12 = 2.

quiz.q: Explain why no graph has exactly one vertex of odd degree.
quiz.a: The total degree sum is 2|E|, which is even. The even-degree vertices contribute an even amount, so the odd-degree vertices must also contribute an even amount. Hence the number of vertices of odd degree must be even; a single odd-degree vertex would make the degree sum odd, which is impossible.

quiz.q: For K<sub>3,4</sub>, give the number of vertices, the number of edges, and the degree of each vertex.
quiz.a: Vertices = 3+4 = 7. Edges = 3×4 = 12. A vertex in the part of size 3 has degree 4; a vertex in the part of size 4 has degree 3.

quiz.q: Is K<sub>2,3</sub> regular? Give a reason.
quiz.a: No. Vertices on the size-2 side have degree 3, and vertices on the size-3 side have degree 2. A regular graph needs one degree for every vertex.

beyond: Not for the exam. Graphs are the data model behind social networks, road routing, package dependency graphs and graph databases. Search for graph databases, network science, spectral graph theory and GraphBLAS to see where these definitions grow. Competitive programming uses the same families in problems on bipartiteness, matching and connectivity.
